faqs.a: It depends on the numbers. A large rebate with a small APR gap favors cash back; a big APR gap over a long term favors the low rate. The only reliable way to know is to compare the total amount paid under both offers — which is exactly what this calculator does.
faqs.q: Is cash back or a low interest rate better?

faqs.a: Usually not. Manufacturers present them as alternatives: take the rebate with standard financing, or take the promotional APR and give up the rebate. Some dealers advertise both, but the fine print almost always forces a choice.
faqs.q: Can I get both the rebate and the low APR?

faqs.a: Yes — usually in favor of the low APR. Interest compounds over time, so the rate gap matters more the longer you borrow. On a 72-month loan, even a 2-point APR difference can outweigh a $2,000 rebate.
faqs.q: Does a longer loan term change the answer?

faqs.a: Totals. A lower monthly payment stretched over a longer term can cost thousands more in interest. Compare the total paid over the same term length to keep the comparison honest.
faqs.q: Should I compare monthly payments or totals?

faqs.a: Early payoff shrinks the interest advantage of the low-APR deal, which can flip the winner toward cash back. If you expect to clear the loan in a year or two, rerun the numbers with that shorter term.
faqs.q: What if I plan to pay the loan off early?

faqs.a: Yes. The same math applies to any financed purchase where you are offered a rebate versus a promotional rate — appliances, furniture, or equipment.
faqs.q: Does this work for purchases other than cars?

cash-back-vs-low-interest-calculator.formula:
Monthly payment M = L x i(1+i)^n / ((1+i)^n - 1), where L = loan amount, i = APR/12, n = months.
Option A: L = price - cash back, financed at the higher APR.
Option B: L = price, financed at the low APR.
Total paid = M x n. The cheaper total wins.
howTo: Enter the cash-back rebate and the APR that comes with it.
Enter the low APR offered without the rebate.
Set the loan term in months, then compare the two totals.
Pick the option with the lower total paid — that is the real saving.
keyFacts: Cash back lowers the amount you finance; a low APR lowers the interest you pay on the full price.
The winner depends on three things: the rebate size, the APR gap, and the loan term.
Longer terms magnify the APR gap, so low-APR deals usually win on 60- to 72-month loans.
A big rebate with only a small APR difference usually favors taking the cash back.
Compare the total amount paid, not the monthly payment — a lower payment can still cost more overall.

cash-back-vs-low-interest-calculator.quickAnswer: On a $30,000 car, a $2,000 rebate at 6.9% APR for 60 months costs $33,187 in total, while 0.9% APR with no rebate costs $30,691. The low-APR deal wins here by $2,496 — but with a bigger rebate or a smaller rate gap, cash back can win. Run your own numbers above.
cash-back-vs-low-interest-calculator.tagline: Compare a cash-back rebate against a low-APR financing deal and see which one really costs less.
cash-back-vs-low-interest-calculator.workedExample:
Price $30,000, $2,000 cash back, 6.9% APR with rebate, 0.9% APR without, 60 months:
1. Option A loan = 30,000 - 2,000 = $28,000. Monthly = $553.11. Total = 553.11 x 60 = $33,186.81.
2. Option B loan = $30,000. Monthly = $511.52. Total = 511.52 x 60 = $30,691.31.
3. Difference: 33,186.81 - 30,691.31 = $2,495.50.
The 0.9% APR deal wins by $2,495.50.
